result: Viral transfection successfully targeted the preBötC and pFL with high specificity. From preBötC injection sites, 82±6% of neurons expressed GFP (n=3), and from pFL injection sites, 81±3% expressed mCitrine (n=3). Transfection sites ranged from ~350–600 µm in diameter, with no labeling found outside injection sites, including the Bötzinger complex.
evaluation: Claims C26-C32 provide direct histological measurements demonstrating successful and specific viral transfection. The high transfection efficiency (>80%), lack of off-target labeling, and independence of responses from injection site size (C29-C30) collectively support the specificity and validity of the targeting approach.

result: Hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons via Alst injection decreased breathing frequency (42 to 22 breaths/min, p=0.008), increased TI and TE, decreased VT and ∫DiaEMG, and induced active expiration during mild hypercapnia. The frequency decrease was quantal rather than continuous, with burstlets appearing during longer respiratory periods. Ultimately, inspiratory activity ceased, leading to apnea.
evaluation: Claims C33-C45 present comprehensive experimental data with appropriate statistical tests (p-values reported, n=8) showing the effects of preBötC silencing. The quantal slowing pattern (C41-C42) is supported by kernel density analysis, and the appearance of burstlets (C43-C44) is documented in Figures 2-3. The progression from decreased breathing to active expiration to apnea is well-documented.

result: Control experiments in non-transfected rats (n=8) showed that Alst injection into the preBötC had no effect on any respiratory parameters (all p>0.1), confirming that the effects observed in transfected rats resulted specifically from AlstR activation.
evaluation: Claims C46-C53 provide essential negative controls demonstrating specificity of the AlstR system. The lack of effects in non-transfected animals (n=8, appropriate statistical tests) validates that observed effects in transfected animals are due to receptor activation rather than non-specific drug effects.

result: Control experiments in non-transfected rats (n=8) showed that 90 µM CNO had no effect on any respiratory parameters (all p>0.1), confirming the specificity of the HM3DR system.
evaluation: Claims C54-C61 provide essential negative controls for the CNO/HM3DR system. The lack of effects in non-transfected animals (n=8, appropriate statistical tests) validates that observed effects in transfected animals are due to receptor activation rather than non-specific drug effects.

result: Depolarizing pFL neurons via CNO (90 µM) in HM3DR-transfected rats (n=8) increased breathing frequency (37 to 42 breaths/min, p=0.04), decreased TE, increased VT, ∫DiaEMG, and ∫GGEMG, and induced expiratory-related ∫AbdEMG (p=0.02), confirming that pFL activation produces active expiration.
evaluation: Claims C62-C70 present comprehensive experimental data with appropriate statistical tests (n=8) showing that pFL activation induces active expiration. The results are consistent with prior optogenetic studies (C69), providing convergent evidence for the role of pFL in active expiration.

result: When pFL neurons were activated by CNO and preBötC neurons were subsequently silenced by Alst, respiratory activity decreased and ultimately resulted in apnea. After inspiratory activity ceased, ∫AbdEMG continued tonically for 15±12 s before disappearing, with rats becoming severely hypercapnic (ETCO2 64.6±14.5 mm Hg).
evaluation: Claims C71-C75 present experimental data (n=8, p=0.008) showing that pFL activation alone cannot sustain active expiration when preBötC is silenced. The tonic AbdEMG duration and hypercapnia levels are well-documented, with appropriate statistical comparisons to control conditions (p=0.7, p=0.8).

result: During recovery from apnea (with CNO-activated pFL and Alst-silenced preBötC), inspiratory activity always returned before expiratory activity. Active expiration did not return until VT reached 3.2±1.7 mL, ∫DiaEMG reached 13.1±8.2 a.u., and ∫GGEMG reached 5.2±4.2 a.u. (n=8). At no time did active expiration occur in the absence of inspiratory activity and chemosensory drive.
evaluation: Claims C76-C79 present critical experimental observations (n=8) demonstrating that pFL cannot independently drive active expiration without preBötC activity or chemosensory drive. The threshold values for active expiration return are quantified, and the consistent temporal sequence (inspiration before expiration) is well-documented in Figure 8.

result: The authors conclude that in adult rats, active expiration is driven by the pFL but requires additional network excitation from either ongoing rhythmic preBötC activity sufficient to drive inspiratory motor output or increased chemosensory drive. The preBötC is the dominant oscillator while the pFL is a subsidiary conditional oscillator, establishing an asymmetrical rather than symmetrical half-center organization.
evaluation: Claims C8, C25, C135, C153-C159 represent the main conclusions synthesized from the experimental data. The conclusion that pFL requires additional excitation is directly supported by the inability to induce active expiration when preBötC is silenced and blood gases are normal (C76-C79, C151-C152). The hierarchical organization is supported by the differential capabilities of the two oscillators demonstrated throughout the experiments.

result: Depressing preBötC activity resulted in quantal slowing of breathing, with burstlets appearing on inspiratory muscle EMGs and airflow during longer respiratory periods. These burstlets represent low-level rhythmogenic activity in the preBötC that, under conditions of increased chemosensory drive, become suprathreshold and are transmitted to motor output.
evaluation: Claims C21-C23, C41-C44, C122-C127 describe the quantal slowing phenomenon and burstlet transmission. The quantal nature is supported by kernel density analysis (C42, Figure 3C), and the appearance of burstlets is documented in Figures 2-3 and 7. The interpretation is consistent with prior work (Kam et al., 2013) and supported by the observation that burstlets can inhibit AbdEMG even when expiratory activity is high (C126).

result: Following hyperpolarization of preBötC neurons, active expiration appeared, potentially due to increased hypoxic/hypercapnic drive to the pFL or disinhibition of the pFL from loss of inhibitory preBötC drive. Subsequently, when inspiratory motor outflow disappeared and hypercapnia/hypoxia increased, active expiration ceased, possibly due to severe hypoxia inhibiting expiratory motor output.
evaluation: Claims C128-C133 present observations (C128 is supported by data) but offer speculative mechanistic explanations (C131-C133). While the appearance of active expiration is documented, the authors acknowledge uncertainty about whether it results from chemosensory drive or disinhibition (C130). The cessation of active expiration during severe hypoxia is observed but the mechanism remains speculative.

result: As rats transitioned from eupnea to apnea following preBötC suppression, ∫AbdEMG transitioned from phasic to tonic. The authors suggest this occurs because expiratory activity is phasic due to periodic inhibition during inspiration, becoming tonic once phasic inspiratory inhibition is lost due to silencing of inhibitory preBötC neurons, implying a significant role for inhibitory preBötC neurons in shaping expiratory output.
evaluation: Claims C136-C142 present observations (C136-C137, C142 are well-documented in Figures 2, 7, 9) and interpretations (C139-C141). The phasic-to-tonic transition is clearly demonstrated, and the interpretation is supported by comparison with prior work in cats (C138, Sears et al., 1982) and by citations to studies on inhibitory preBötC neurons (C140). The asymmetry between eupnea-to-apnea and apnea-to-eupnea transitions (C142) provides additional support.

result: Following apnea during mechanical ventilation (with CNO-activated pFL and Alst-silenced preBötC), breathing recovery occurred in three phases: (1) no activity even off ventilator, (2) spontaneous breathing only when off ventilator (likely due to chemosensory drive overcoming waning Alst effect), and (3) spontaneous breathing during ventilation once Alst wore off. In all phases, inspiratory activity returned before expiratory activity, and active expiration never occurred without inspiration. Since blood gases were normal, the loss of expiratory activity was not due to excessive hypoxia/hypercapnia.
evaluation: Claims C143-C152 describe detailed observations from the recovery protocol (n=8, documented in Figure 8). The three-phase recovery pattern is well-documented, and the consistent temporal sequence (inspiration before expiration) is clearly demonstrated. The inference that normal blood gases rule out hypoxia/hypercapnia as the cause (C152) is reasonable given the measurements shown in Figure 8.

result: The authors address the potential confound of retrograde transfection by AAV2/5, asserting that results are unlikely to be confounded because: (1) no labeling was found outside injection sites, (2) CNO was applied to the ventral surface with limited penetration, and (3) effects match those from optogenetic studies using non-retrogradely transported lentivirus.
evaluation: Claims C80-C85 address an important methodological concern. The evidence against retrograde transfection confounds is strong: histological analysis shows no off-target labeling (C82, Figure 1E-F), the drug application method limits spread (C83), and convergent results with optogenetics using lentivirus (C85) provide independent validation. However, the claim about limited CNO penetration (C83) is an inference rather than direct measurement.

result: The manuscript is based on the hypothesis that breathing in mammals results from interaction of two oscillators: the preBötC driving inspiration and the pFL driving active expiration. In mammals at rest, the preBötC drives the underlying rhythm, while the pFL turns on during increased metabolic demand. In adult rats, the preBötC can generate inspiratory rhythm while the pFL is quiescent.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C10, C16-C18 establish the conceptual framework based on prior literature. These claims are well-supported by extensive citations and represent established knowledge in the field. The experimental work in this manuscript tests and refines this framework.

result: NK1R-expressing neurons in the parafacial region show respiratory-rhythmic activity from third trimester in utero to adulthood. These neurons have been designated as e-pF (embryonic), pFRG (postnatal), and pFL (adult) at different developmental stages. The authors postulate these represent one population studied at different time points. These neurons are almost exclusively glutamatergic.
evaluation: Claims C86-C93 synthesize prior literature about the developmental identity of parafacial respiratory neurons. The claims are well-supported by multiple citations (C86-C89, C91-C92), and the parsimonious interpretation of a single population (C90) is reasonable though explicitly stated as a postulate. The glutamatergic nature is supported by citation (C91) and the authors' own data (C93, Figure 1D).

result: In embryonic mice, the pFL is rhythmic before the preBötC forms (E14.5). At E15.5, the preBötC forms and couples to the pFL. The two oscillators can function independently (demonstrated by transverse section, CNQX, or riluzole), and their rhythmic output is a convolution of the faster pFL and slower preBötC rhythms. The pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while preBötC bursting (inhibitory and excitatory) both inhibits and excites pFL neurons.
evaluation: Claims C96-C103 summarize prior work on embryonic respiratory control, primarily from Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009. These claims are well-supported by citations and Figure 9A provides a clear schematic. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.

result: In postnatal rats, the glutamatergic pFL provides excitatory drive to the preBötC, while preBötC bursting inhibits and excites different pFL neuron subsets. Both oscillators can function independently (preBötC in transverse slices, pFL after opioid suppression of preBötC). Immediately after birth, the pFL appears to drive respiratory rhythm, possibly to protect against opioid surge during birth. Shortly after birth (~P2-P4), the breathing CPG becomes driven by the preBötC and remains so throughout life.
evaluation: Claims C104-C112 summarize prior work on postnatal respiratory control with appropriate citations. The developmental transition from pFL-driven to preBötC-driven breathing is well-documented in the cited literature. The speculation about opioid protection (C110) is appropriately qualified. Figure 9B provides clear schematic support.

result: In juvenile rats, the preBötC and pFL are reciprocally coupled but differentially affected by fentanyl (shifts to expiratory-dominant pattern) and can be independently suppressed by Breuer-Hering reflexes (BHDR or BHIR).
evaluation: Claims C113-C114 summarize prior work from Janczewski and Feldman, 2006, with appropriate citation and schematic support in Figure 9C. These claims accurately represent the cited literature.

result: In adult rats, the preBötC is the dominant oscillator active at rest, while the pFL is a subsidiary conditional oscillator that is quiescent at rest. The pFL drives active expiration when preBötC activity is concurrent or reduced and appropriate inputs are present (exogenous receptor activation or altered blood gases). In the absence of preBötC activity, chemosensory drive can drive active expiration, though abdominal activity becomes tonic. The pFL cannot independently drive respiratory movements when preBötC is silenced or when preBötC activity is low with normal blood gases. Excitatory drive from preBötC to pFL likely occurs through an intermediate relay such as the pFV.
evaluation: Claims C115-C121 synthesize the current study's findings with prior work. The dominant/subsidiary oscillator relationship is directly supported by the experimental data (particularly C76-C79, C119-C120). The role of chemosensory drive (C118) is supported by the tonic AbdEMG during severe hypercapnia. The indirect connectivity through pFV (C121) is a reasonable inference based on anatomical data (Tan et al., 2010) and is appropriately qualified as "most likely."

result: The authors speculate that the asymmetrical organization of respiratory oscillators may be relevant to other neural networks with hierarchically organized coupled oscillators, such as those underlying flexion and extension in locomotion. The developmental and state-dependent changes in preBötC-pFL interactions represent additional complexity in understanding respiratory control.
evaluation: Claims C160-C161 present broader implications and perspectives. C160 is appropriately qualified as speculative ("may be relevant") with citations to locomotion literature. C161 is a reasonable summary statement supported by the developmental review in Figure 9. These claims are appropriately cautious and well-contextualized.

result: The pharmacogenetic tools used in this study (AlstR activated by Alst to silence preBötC neurons, and HM3DR activated by CNO to depolarize pFL neurons) are established methods from prior work.
evaluation: Claims C19-C20 describe established pharmacogenetic tools with appropriate citations (Tan et al., 2008; Armbruster et al., 2007). These are methodological claims supported by prior literature and validated by the control experiments (C46-C61).

result: The parafacial regions (RTN and pFRG/e-PF) contain overlapping subpopulations expressing NK1R, Phox2b, and VGlut2, and are chemosensitive. They can be functionally separated: pFV provides drive to expiration while pFL contains a presumptive expiratory rhythm generator and neurons with respiratory rhythmic behavior. The pFL and pFV do not contain inhibitory neurons, so any inhibitory actions occur through intermediate relays, possibly in the preBötC or BötC.
evaluation: Claims C11-C15, C94-C95 provide anatomical and functional context from prior literature with appropriate citations. The functional separation of pFL and pFV is supported by multiple studies. The conclusion about indirect inhibitory actions (C95) is a reasonable inference based on the absence of inhibitory markers in these regions.

result: The abstract claims are directly supported by the detailed experimental results: hyperpolarizing preBötC neurons decreased inspiratory activity, initiated active expiration, and ultimately led to apnea; depolarizing pFL neurons produced active expiration at rest but not when inspiratory activity was suppressed.
evaluation: Claims C3-C7 are abstract-level summaries that are directly supported by the detailed experimental data presented in C33-C79. These represent accurate high-level summaries of the main findings.

result: The authors confirmed that pFL activation initiates active expiration, consistent with prior optogenetic and disinhibition studies.
evaluation: Claim C24 is directly supported by the experimental data in C62-C70 and is consistent with prior work (Pagliardini et al., 2011; Huckstepp et al., 2015). This represents a confirmatory finding using a different methodological approach.
